But what about the difference between consistent *dependent* and consistent *independent?* What is the reasoning behind these naming conventions?

To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

- First, consider the following system.
${3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4$
This system has *infinitely many* solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)
In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ can be expressed as
$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
${y = 2x + 1; y = 1 - x$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
